pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Diet, Exercise & Lifestyle

- **Standards — UK (DfE Y6 'Animals, including humans'):** "recognise the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the way their bodies function".

- **Standards — US (no direct NGSS PE):** Health/lifestyle impacts are handled in US health education standards rather than NGSS science PEs; the biological grounding relates to body-systems function (MS-LS1-3). Treat as UK-led.

- **Operational details:** This is an APPLIED, cause-and-effect topic that draws on the systems children have learned (circulatory, digestive, muscular). The organising idea is that lifestyle CHOICES affect how well body systems function: a balanced diet supplies the right nutrients and energy; exercise strengthens the heart and muscles and helps maintain a healthy weight; harmful substances (drugs, alcohol, tobacco) damage organs and impair function. Teach it as evidence-based reasoning linking a choice to a bodily effect (exercise → heart beats faster now, gets stronger over time; too much sugar/fat → weight gain, strain on the heart), grounded in the circulatory/nutrition topics rather than as moralising 'good vs bad' lists. Handle drugs age-appropriately and factually. A working-scientifically strand fits well (measuring pulse before/after exercise; interpreting simple health data).

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional, applied). A Y6 child can list healthy/unhealthy choices (Tier A); the target is EXPLAINING the impact — linking a specific choice to how a body system functions, using evidence — which is the transitional reasoning step.
bestPractices: Teach it as CAUSE-AND-EFFECT on body function (choice → effect on a system), not as moralising 'good vs bad' food/behaviour lists.
Ground every impact in the systems children already know (exercise on the heart from the circulatory topic; diet on energy from the nutrition topic) so reasoning is mechanistic.
Use real measurement (pulse before/after exercise, interpreting simple health data) to make the impact evidence-based and personal.
Distinguish immediate effects (heart rate rises during exercise) from long-term effects (heart gets stronger, weight changes over time).
Handle drugs, alcohol and tobacco factually and age-appropriately, focusing on how they affect body function rather than fear messaging.
Emphasise that everyone's body is affected by choices, avoiding stigma around weight or health status.
keyRepresentations: A choice→effect diagram linking diet/exercise/substances to a body system
A 'lifestyle over time' set of meters (fitness, healthy weight, organ function)
A body figure showing which system each choice affects
Cross-links back to the circulatory and nutrition representations
commonMisconceptions: Treating the topic as 'good vs bad' foods/behaviours rather than understanding the mechanism of impact on body function.
Thinking exercise only builds muscles, missing its effect on the heart, lungs and healthy weight.
Believing effects are only immediate (or only long-term), rather than both (heart rate now, strengthening over time).
Assuming 'healthy' means thin or that weight alone measures health, rather than how well systems function.
Thinking small amounts of harmful substances have no effect on how the body works.

learn.summary: Help 10–11 year-olds EXPLAIN (not just list) how lifestyle choices affect how body systems function, using cause-and-effect reasoning grounded in the circulatory, digestive and muscular systems they already know. The teaching core is linking a specific choice (exercise, diet balance, harmful substances) to a bodily effect — for example exercise strengthens the heart and muscles and also benefits mental health — distinguishing immediate effects (heart rate rises now) from long-term effects (heart strengthens, resting pulse lowers, weight changes), and backing the reasoning with real measurement (pulse before/after exercise). Treat drugs, alcohol and tobacco factually and age-appropriately, and avoid moralising 'good vs bad' lists or stigma around weight.

activities.title: Lifestyle simulator: run a body over time by changing choices
feedback: If a learner only notices the instant heart-rate change, prompt: let simulated weeks pass — what happens to the heart-strength and weight meters over time, not just right now?
If a learner frames it as 'good food vs bad food', redirect: which system did this change affect, and how? Describe the mechanism, not a good/bad label.
If a learner treats a small amount of a harmful substance as having no effect, have them toggle it and read the organ-function meter, then explain what changed.

Reinforce correct reasoning by asking the learner to name the organ or body system (heart and blood vessels, lungs, muscles, digestive system) behind each meter movement, treating weight as a measure rather than a system, and link it back to the circulatory (heart, blood and lungs) or nutrition topic.
Note for the learner that the meters are an illustrative model of how choices tend to affect systems over time, not precise physiological numbers.
activities.rationale: Letting learners vary choices and watch systems recompute turns an abstract 'impact' into an observed consequence they caused, supporting the transitional step from listing choices to explaining mechanisms. Live meters for heart rate, fitness, weight and organ function are concrete interaction examples that make the cause→effect link visible; they are offered as one way to make the mechanism felt, not as the only way to teach it.
sourceClaims: Exercise raises heart rate immediately and strengthens the heart and muscles over time; a balanced diet supplies needed nutrients and energy; harmful substances impair organ function — the cause-effect basis for KS2 lifestyle-impact teaching.
learnerActions: Set a character's choices using controls: an exercise/activity level, a diet-balance control, and toggles for harmful substances (tobacco, alcohol, misused or illegal drugs). Medicines are also drugs and, used correctly, can help the body.
Push the exercise level up and observe the live heart-rate meter climb immediately.
Let a few simulated weeks pass and watch the 'heart & muscle strength' and 'healthy weight' meters change over time.
Then lower activity and set the diet to very sugary/fatty, and watch the weight and heart-strain meters move the other way.
Add tobacco and observe a lung-function meter fall.
Run the SAME starting body twice with different choice settings and compare how differently it ends up functioning.
In words, state one immediate effect and one long-term effect of a choice you set, naming which body system it affected.
activities.intendedInsight: A lifestyle choice is a cause that changes how a specific body system functions, with both immediate and longer-term effects. In the model, the same starting body can end up functioning very differently because of the choices made; in real life, genes, age and other factors also play a part.

activities.title: Pulse before and after exercise (real measurement)
feedback: If a learner predicts no change, have them compare their before/after numbers and explain the difference they recorded.
If a learner says 'exercise doesn't change anything inside', point to their own recovery time and the fact that the heart is a muscle responding to activity.
Encourage comparing recovery times rather than ranking people — frame differences as fitness of the heart, avoiding stigma.
activities.rationale: Real measurement makes the immediate effect evidence-based and personal, and grounds the simulator's modelled behaviour in the learner's own body. Predicting first surfaces the misconception that internal function doesn't change.
sourceClaims: Exercise raises heart rate immediately and strengthens the heart and muscles over time; a balanced diet supplies needed nutrients and energy; harmful substances impair organ function — the cause-effect basis for KS2 lifestyle-impact teaching.
learnerActions: Measure and record your resting pulse (beats per minute).
PREDICT what your pulse will do after exercise and why.
Do one minute of vigorous activity such as star jumps.
Measure your pulse again immediately afterwards.
Time how long it takes to return to your resting rate.
Compare results across people and discuss why a fitter person's pulse tends to recover faster and why their resting rate is often lower.
Connect what you measured to the simulator: find the same rise reflected in the on-screen heart-rate meter.
activities.intendedInsight: The heart's response to exercise is real, measurable and personal: heart rate rises during activity and recovers afterwards, and greater fitness is linked to a lower resting rate and faster recovery.

activities.title: Explore-a-body: reveal how each choice affects a system, with myth-busters
feedback: If a learner thinks exercise only builds arm/leg muscles, open the heart reveal and the 'exercise only builds muscles?' myth-buster, and have them restate the internal effect.
If a learner judges health by appearance, surface the point that health is how well systems function, not body shape.
Prompt learners to link each reveal back to the circulatory or nutrition topic they already studied.
activities.rationale: A tap/select-to-reveal body teaches the cause→effect facts clearly and targets named misconceptions directly, serving as a scaffold for the links. It presents fixed revealed facts rather than letting the learner vary inputs, so it builds the vocabulary of links but does not by itself provide the manipulable cause-effect experience.
sourceClaims: Exercise raises heart rate immediately and strengthens the heart and muscles over time; a balanced diet supplies needed nutrients and energy; harmful substances impair organ function — the cause-effect basis for KS2 lifestyle-impact teaching.
learnerActions: Select the heart to reveal what regular exercise does to it (strengthens it, lowers resting heart rate).
Select the lungs to reveal how smoking affects them.
Select muscles and the digestive links to reveal how diet balance supplies energy and nutrients.
Reveal that regular exercise also benefits mental health, not only the heart and muscles.
Open myth-buster prompts such as 'Does exercise only build visible muscles?' and read the correction.
For each revealed link, say aloud which choice is the cause and which system is affected, and whether the effect is immediate, long-term, or both.
activities.intendedInsight: Each lifestyle choice maps to specific effects on specific body systems — exercise is more than bigger limb muscles (it strengthens the heart, lowers resting pulse and supports mental health), and harmful substances impair organ function.

activities.title: Consolidate: match, categorise and explain WHY
feedback: If an answer only says 'it's healthy/unhealthy', push for the specific system and how it is affected.
If a learner confuses immediate and long-term effects, have them separate 'what happens now' from 'what happens over weeks'.
Confirm answers that correctly name the mechanism and the system involved.
activities.rationale: Matching, categorisation and why-questions consolidate the applied reasoning and reveal whether the learner can state a mechanism. Recognition-and-selection tasks check understanding but do not themselves elicit the independent, constructed explanation, so pair them with the written-sentence step.
learnerActions: Match each lifestyle choice to its effect on a specific body system.
Categorise choices by whether they help or harm how a system functions.
Answer explanation questions that require the MECHANISM (e.g. why does regular exercise lower resting heart rate?), not just a 'good/bad' label.
For at least one item, write a sentence naming the choice, the system affected, and whether the effect is immediate or long-term.
activities.intendedInsight: Explaining a lifestyle impact means stating the mechanism linking a choice to a body system's function, distinguishing immediate from long-term effects.

activities.title: Ask the expert: questions for a GP or sports coach
feedback: If answers drift into fear messaging or moralising, refocus on how the substance or choice affects body function.
Prompt the learner to connect each answer back to the circulatory or nutrition systems.
Encourage follow-up questions that separate immediate from long-term effects.
activities.rationale: An in-role expert conversation may motivate the reasoning through the learner's own questions and can handle the drugs topic sensitively and factually. It is offered as a motivating complement; it is less focused than hands-on measurement or the simulator for drilling the core impact-reasoning objective.
learnerActions: Think of your own questions, such as 'What happens to my heart if I train regularly?' or 'Why is smoking bad for my lungs?'
Ask an in-role GP or coach persona and listen to factual, age-appropriate answers.
Follow up to find out whether an effect is immediate or long-term, and which system it touches.
Summarise one answer in your own words, naming the choice, the system and the effect.
activities.intendedInsight: Lifestyle-impact reasoning can be driven by a learner's own curiosity, including sensitive topics like drugs, handled factually.

constraints: Target skill is EXPLAINING impact (linking a specific choice to how a body system functions, with evidence), not merely listing healthy/unhealthy choices.
Teach as cause-and-effect on body function, not as moralising 'good vs bad' food/behaviour lists.

Ground each impact in a body system learners know (for example the heart, blood vessels and lungs, the digestive system, and muscles) so reasoning stays mechanistic; some effects, such as smoking on the lungs or alcohol on the liver and brain, involve organs beyond the circulatory, digestive and muscular systems.
Distinguish immediate effects (heart rate rises during exercise) from long-term effects (heart strengthens, resting pulse lowers, weight changes over time).
Include exercise's benefit to mental health, as required by the objective evidence, alongside heart and muscle effects.
Handle drugs, alcohol and tobacco factually and age-appropriately, focusing on body function rather than fear messaging.
Avoid stigma: do not equate health with thinness or body shape; frame health as how well systems function; compare fitness without ranking individuals.

The explore-a-body reveal and consolidation tasks are scaffolds: reveals present fixed facts and selection tasks check recognition — neither by itself elicits an independent, learner-constructed explanation, so include steps where the learner states or writes the mechanism themselves.

Pulse measurement varies by individual and effort; treat it as a personal observation, not a fixed rule — recovery and resting-rate differences illustrate fitness, not a verdict on a person. Do not claim a fitter person's pulse 'rises less' during vigorous activity, which the sources do not support.
Simulator meters are an illustrative model of tendencies over time, not precise physiology.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

One cited source (BBC Bitesize claim) is marked verified:false in the row; the DfE statutory-requirement claim is marked verified:true. Treat the cause-effect claim as unverified in the legacy record.

The mental-health benefit of exercise is grounded in the objective evidence and the assessment correctAnswer, not in the cited BBC claim, which does not mention it; it is taught as an objective-required fact, not as source-verified.

The legacy row asserted that a static list 'can't' make impact felt and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these comparative/necessity claims are not established by the available sources and have been softened to affordance-based descriptions.
Simulator meter behaviour (e.g. exact weight/heart-strain/organ-function dynamics) is a pedagogical model; keep any modelled numbers plausible and framed as illustrative, not precise physiology.
The claim that a fitter person's pulse 'rises less' during the same activity was removed as unsupported; only faster recovery and a lower resting rate are grounded in the source.

assess.poeTask: Have each student measure their resting pulse, do one minute of vigorous activity (star jumps), then measure again and time how long it takes to return to resting. Ask them first to PREDICT what the pulse will do and why. Seeing it rise and then recover — faster in fitter students — makes the heart's response to exercise concrete, challenging 'exercise doesn't change anything inside'.
probeDeeper: Two people have the same-sized arm muscles, but one exercises daily — what's different inside their bodies?
Is there a food you'd call completely 'bad'? What happens if you eat even a healthy food in huge amounts?
Why does a very fit person's heart beat fewer times per minute at rest?
Besides the body, what else does regular exercise affect — and how would you notice?
assess.correctAnswer: It's not true. The heart is a muscle, and regular exercise makes it stronger so it pumps more blood per beat; this lowers the resting heart rate and delivers oxygen more efficiently, even at rest. Exercise also benefits the lungs, helps maintain a healthy weight, and improves mental health — it's far more than bigger limb muscles.

errorPatterns.pattern: Exercise only makes your visible muscles bigger — nothing changes inside
errorPatterns.nextMove: The heart is a muscle too and gets stronger with exercise; compare a fit and an unfit person's resting pulse to make the internal change visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: Exercise just makes your arms and legs bigger — nothing changes inside.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Denies internal effects; talks only about arm/leg muscle size

errorPatterns.pattern: Some foods are simply 'good' and others 'bad', whatever the amount
errorPatterns.nextMove: It's balance and amount that matter; even fats and sugars have roles, and too much of anything (including 'healthy' food) can harm.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Labels foods as absolutely good or bad, ignoring quantity and balance

errorPatterns.pattern: Being thin means being healthy (health = appearance)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Health is about how well the body's systems function — heart, lungs, mind — not appearance; a thin person can be unfit and vice versa.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Equates good health with body shape or slimness

responseLevels.gap: Sees exercise as only muscle-building and judges health by appearance; labels foods good/bad absolutely.
responseLevels.full: Explains exercise strengthens the heart and other systems with effects that persist at rest, frames diet as balance and quantity, and connects lifestyle to how body systems function.
responseLevels.partial: Knows exercise is 'good for you' and diet matters, but can't name a specific internal effect (heart) or explain balance over absolute good/bad foods.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Someone says 'exercise just makes your arm and leg muscles bigger — it doesn't really change anything inside your body.' Is that true? What does regular exercise do to your heart, and why would that matter even when you're sitting still later?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands lifestyle effects points to internal, systemic changes (heart strengthens, resting pulse drops). A child who sees exercise as only cosmetic muscle-building cannot explain any benefit that persists at rest.
